items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Next week, when the House
resumes on Tuesday, 24 June,  the Government will look to progress the Appropriation
(2013/14 Supplementary Estimates) Bill, the Companies and Limited Partnerships
Amendment Bill, and a number of other items on the Order Paper. Wednesday is a
members’ day.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Can I ask the Leader of
the House whether there is any intent to progress the Crimes (Match -fixing)
Amendment Bill before the House rises?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes.
Economic Growth—Progress and Reports
1. CLAUDETTE HAUITI (National) to the Minister of Finance: What reports has
he received on progress in building a growing economy that can support more jobs and
higher incomes for New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Statistics New Zealand this morning
issued GDP figures for March. It confirms that the economy is continuing to perform
well, growing by 1 percent in the 3 months to 31 March and by 3.8 percent in the 12
months up to the end of March, which is good news for New Zealanders looking for
higher incomes and more jobs. Economic growth was reasonably broad -based, with
positive contributions from construction, mining, agriculture, retail trade, and
accommodation. It is the latest in a run of encouraging  economic indicators, including
higher levels of business and consumer confidence. I want to pay tribute to the strong
and stable leadership of the Prime Minister, who has the unanimous support of a united
caucus. This has been instrumental in the Government’s successful economic policy.

items.speaker: Claudette Hauiti
items.text: How is the growing economy translating into real benefits for
New Zealanders and their families?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Most people do not measure their economic prospects i n
terms of GDP; they measure it in terms of more jobs and higher incomes. In the past
year alone 84,000 more jobs were created, and the Budget last month forecast an
additional 170,000 new jobs by mid -2018. If we stick with the Government’s
programme, the average full-time wage is expected to rise by $7,600, to $62,300, over
the next 4 years. This follows a $3,000 increase in the average wage over the past 3
years.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If that answer was so compellingly valid, how c ome the
Māngere section of the National Party rejected it when it was put to it by the questioner
when she sought the nomination there?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In so far as there may be some ministerial responsibility, the Hon
Bill English.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, I am going to be going and talking not just to the
Māngere branch of the National Party but to all those former Labour and New Zealand
First voters in Māngere who are starting to think about voting National.
18714 Questions for Oral Answer 19 Jun 2014

items.speaker: Claudette Hauiti
items.text: Kia ora. How does New Zealand’s latest economy growth
compare with growth in other developed economies around the world?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: New Zealand continues to be one of the better -performing
developed economies. Our 3.8 percent growth rate was the third -highest in the OECD
club of developed economies. By comparison, Australia grew about the same at 3.5
percent, the UK grew 3.1 percent,  the United States grew 2 percent, Canada grew 2
percent, Japan grew 2.8 percent, and the euro area grew 0.9 percent. So New Zealand is
doing reasonably well, but we need to continue to work on sustaining these growth rates
beyond the normal cycle so that more households can benefit from consistently rising
incomes.

items.speaker: Claudette Hauiti
items.text: How does New Zealand’s current economic performance compare
with the indicators this Government inherited in late 2008?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The indicators have improved in part because of the
improved economic cycle and in part because of good Government policy. The balance
of payments deficit, for instance, in 2008 was minus 7 percent of GDP, and it is
currently 2.8 percent. The Government is  on track to Budget surplus next year. In 2008
we faced never -ending deficits and soaring Government debt. The cost of living has
risen by just 1.5 percent a year. In 2008 it was rising by more than 5 percent per year,
when the cost of living was out of control. Floating mortgage interest rates are a bit over
6 percent today. In 2008 they reached almost 11 percent.
Hon David Cunliffe—Immigration Inquiry on Constituent’s Behalf
2. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Leader of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: Is
he concerned about rising inequality in New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As the member well knows, the
most recent research shows that income inequality is not rising in New Zealand. I know
that members are worried about other forms of inequality, and so am I, particularly the
inequality between the support for David Cunliffe in the Labour caucus—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That may not help the order of the House.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Given those comments, does the Prime Minister stand by his
statement in the United States that National has known for 2 weeks ab out the existence
of a letter from me to Mr Donghua Liu, and how does he reconcile that with Mr
English’s comments that senior National Party MPs did not know about it?
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It may be Thursday afternoon and some members may be
keen to return to their electorates early, and if the noise keeps up to this level, somebody
will. I will hear the point of order from the Hon Gerry Brownlee, and I remind members
it is a point of order.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My point is simply this.
Although the Acting Prime Minister on behalf of the Prime Minister is happy to answer
the question, it is very wide of the wickets and perhaps is an in dicator of the capacity
inside our opponents to deliver—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I reminded members to my left, before the point of order
was started, that it is a point of order. So would the member please finish his point of
order.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: No, I think I made the point.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: It was quite clear at the end of the Acting Prime Minister’s
answers that he introduced this material. It is perfectly within the Standing Orders to ask
questions in response to that.
19 Jun 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 18715

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Acting Prime Minister in answering certainly extended the
scope. I invite him now to answer the question that was asked by the Hon David
Cunliffe.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I understand that the letter was in the public arena because it
was requested under the Official Information Act by a number of media outlets and that
prior to that, I am advised today, it came to the notice of a Minister who was answering
oral questions in the House when the Leader of the Opposition was on his high horse
about cronyism between Maurice Williamson and why he should be sacked because of
it.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Given that the New Zealand Herald  journalist concerned
requested the lette r that we have been referring to regarding Mr Donghua Liu only on
Monday of this week, how is it that he knew about it for the last 2 weeks?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is apparent that the New Zealand Herald journalist was
more concerned about understanding the background to these events than the Leader of
the Opposition was, who had been vigorously prosecuting the campaign against Mr Liu
and Maurice Williamson for about 3 weeks. He should have done the same thing —that
is, find out the informati on himself in the same way that the New Zealand Herald
journalist did.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. That was a very specific
question and it was not addressed in the answer by the Acting Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In my opinion, and to the best of my ability to hear the answer, the
answer was adequately addressed by—[Interruption] Order! The member will remain in
his seat while I am on my feet. It would be helpful if I could more clearly listen to the
answer. That would certainly require less interjection from the left.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Just to clarify, are you
asking me to repeat the question because you were unable to hear the answer?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I am not. I am saying that the question has been addressed, but I
am inviting the member to continue with further supplementary questions if he so
wishes.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I will. Thank you. Given that the New Zealand Herald
journalist concerned requested the letter in only the last 48 hours, how did the Prime
Minister know about it for the last 2 weeks?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, the member would need to ask the Prime Minister that
question—[Interruption]—and I understand that he is being asked that question, and no
doubt he will answer it. But that member seems to be riding flat out on his high horse
towards the pet-food factory.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does he think his Mini ster of Finance misled listeners on
Radio New Zealand this morning when he said that senior National Party MPs did not
know about the letter?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No. I was speaking for myself. I was aware of the letter
yesterday and, as John Campbell said, like many other New Zealanders, I was shocked,
I was stunned, I could not believe it, and I am surprised that the member wants to keep
talking about it.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Was it reasonable for the Prime Minister to as sume that at
some point, as the arguments were evolving, the Leader of the Opposition might have
outed himself before the Official Information Act process did it for him?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Prime Minister probably assumed that the Leader of the
Opposition, when he was vigorously prosecuting the resignation of a Government
Minister, knew what he was doing and was familiar with the background to the issue.
But it appears that, like Labour Party policies, it was unresearched, critical details were
18716 Questions for Oral Answer 19 Jun 2014
missing, and the Leader of the Opposition now has to take responsibility for yet another
mess, which his caucus is pretty upset about.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: On which occasion has the Hon Bill En glish been misleading
the public —when he said on Radio New Zealand National this morning that senior
National Party MPs did not know about the letter or when he has just acknowledged in
the House, on behalf of the Prime Minister, that the Prime Minister did?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No. I was asked my view about that issue on Radio New
Zealand National and I answered to the best of my knowledge, which is that I did not
know about that letter, and I did not know whether other Ministers knew about it. The
critical thing is that I knew more than David Cunliffe, when I knew almost nothing.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Would he advise the Leader of the Opposition to make a
thorough check of his party files and other matters, to ensure that all declarations around
donations are as well recorded as this particular letter?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is a good try, but on this occasion there is certainly no
responsibility there.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Further to the Acting Prime  Minister’s last answer, can the
House take it that he now thinks “to the best of somebody’s knowledge, based on the
information available to them at the time” is an absolutely right and proper answer?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Actually, I think the answer to that is yes. But, of course,
when I said to the media that I did not know about the letter I was not testing the trust of
New Zealanders in the way that David Cunliffe is now. He said he would not tell us
where he lived. He said it was a doer -upper, and it was a mansion. He announced
policies without—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] The member has a right to ask a
supplementary question.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Members may not like the questions, but people are li stening
to them. Can he tell the House whether who knew what or when changes the fact that
the Leader of the Opposition tried to hide the material facts?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Again, I do not believe there is any ministerial responsibility.
[Interruption] Could the House please settle down.
Banking Sector—Anti-competitive Behaviour
3. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Commerce
items.text: Has he received any reports on  anti-competitive behaviour in the banking
sector?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I am not aware of receiving any
specific reports, but if the member has examples of anti -competitive behaviour in the
banking sector these should be directed to and taken to the Commerce Commission.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does he think it appropriate for a bank to simply terminate
a company’s accounts with that bank without g iving any reason whatsoever for doing
so; if not, why not, as the Minister?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: In those circumstances the organisation concerned has a
number of remedies. It could go to the bank. It could go to the Banking Ombudsman or
to some other disputes resolution service. If something uncompetitive was happening,
then the organisation should take its complaint to the Commerce Commission.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Should a company called IMEX Ltd, which provides
remittance services in New Zealand, Australia, and the Pacific Islands have cause for
concern about anti -competitive behaviour when one of its direct competitors, namely
Westpac, with whom IMEX banks, writes to it terminating its accounts without
providing any reason for doing so?
19 Jun 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 18717

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I just repeat my previous answer. Those issues are between that
organisation and its bank, whoever that was, and regardless of who that bank is, that
bank has courses to remedy, or make complaint about, those issues that the member
raises.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If it became apparent that Westpac had been engaging in
anti-competitive banking behaviour, would he, as the responsible Minister and on behalf
of his Government, support ma king another bank, such as Kiwibank, the Government’s
bank rather than allow this to go on with the Government’s support?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: The member is confused. He does not understand the
Commerce Act. The question was primarily about ant i-competitive behaviour. The
Commerce Act looks after that. The Commerce Commission looks after those particular
issues. So if the member has issues around that—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: —he should go to the Commerce Commission.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have a point of order.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Rather than take that insult, I asked in particular, given that
he is the Minister respo nsible in terms of giving advice to the Government, whether the
Government would keep its account with Westpac. That is the question I want
answered. Surely that is what I referred to.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have a little bit of sympathy for the member.  The question has
been answered. I think it has been addressed, but I will allow the member an additional
supplementary question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Seeing that where the Government’s account is could
become an issue for the Government—it is currently with Westpac—and if it was found
that Westpac was engaging in anti -competitive behaviour, would he then recommend
that the Government move its account to a bank such as Kiwibank?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I have no responsibility for whomever the Government uses for
its banking arrangements.
Christchurch Hospitals—Redevelopment
4. Dr PAUL HUTCHISON (National —Hunua) to the Minister of Health : What
progress is being made on the Christchurch Hospitals’ redevelopment?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Design plans are now entering the final
stage of development, and construction is expected to  begin in September as part of a
$650 million —plus investment in Canterbury. Once complete, the new Christchurch
Hospital will boast new operating theatres with around 400 beds, an expanded intensive
care unit, a new emergency department, and a rooftop hel ipad. Canterbury District
Health Board is holding a public meeting tonight to update Cantabrians on progress, and
the district health board is very keen for the public to attend.

items.speaker: Dr Paul Hutchison
items.text: What progress has been made at the Burwood health campus?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: At Burwood construction is now under way. When
completed, that hospital will have 23 extra beds, an extended radiology department, and
a new outpatient department able to manage 80,000 outpatients a year.  The Government
is committed to providing Cantabrians with top-quality health facilities.
Economy—Income Gap, Regional Economies, Growth, and Child Poverty
5. Hon DAVID PARKER (Deputy Leader —Labour) to the Minister of Finance:
Which of the statements, if any, by NZIER chief economist, Shamubeel Eaqub, does he
agree with most: that interest rate rises will punish the provinces, that “one of the
biggest issues of this generation is the wide ning gap between the haves and have -nots”,
or that “The gaps opening up in New Zealand are really big across geographical, race
and education lines”?
18718 Questions for Oral Answer 19 Jun 2014

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I do not agree with those statements.
I do agree with other statements made by the same commentator when he said: “It reeks
of xenophobia … poor policy making … a populist knee -jerk reaction” and “sloppy.”
That was Shamubeel Eaqub talking about Labour’s housing policies.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is the Minister aware that over the past 5 years there are 7,800
fewer people employed in the Waikato, there has been a loss of 7,300 people employed
in Manawatū-Wanganui and 2,100 people employe d in Wellington, and there are 6,200
fewer people employed in Southland, or is he so out of touch that he does not know
what is going on outside Auckland and Christchurch?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I disagree with that, and the member is so o ut of touch
he cannot remember there was a thing called the global financial crisis. So when he
compares numbers prior to the biggest recession in 30 years with the recovery
afterwards, then of course he is going to find that in some respects some numbers have
still yet to improve. But in an economy that produced 84,000 new jobs over the last
year, that has closed up those gaps very considerably and probably faster than people
expected.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Given that two -thirds of GDP growt h is coming from
construction activity, which makes GDP growth other than construction closer to 1
percent than 3 percent, what is his plan to boost economic growth, aside from another
earthquake?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, I am aware of the  numbers around housing and it is
slightly ironic that the member’s party has spent all year castigating the Government for
not building enough houses, and now that they are being built apparently it is bad for
the economy. Saying that we should not count the benefits of construction is a bit like
saying that if you take out the tries the All Blacks scored, they did not actually win the
game.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is he really so out of touch with New Zealanders that he denies
inequality is r ising when homeownership rates are at the lowest in 50 years and
dropping and child poverty is rising?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, as I think the House has discussed before, most
measures of income inequality in New Zealand show that it is no t getting worse. It is
simply not the case that the rich are getting richer and the poor are getting poorer. When
the member talks about inequality of ownership of assets, then I would hope that his
party will see its way to supporting the Government’s pro gramme to free up the supply
of housing, because a fast -rising housing market is likely to drive inequality in the
ownership of assets because it favours those in the market as against those who are out
of it. In that respect we agree on the objective —that is, a slower-rising housing market.
It is a shame we have not been able to agree on the tools, because the Government has
got good tools for addressing that driver of asset ownership.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does the income inequality figure that he just referred to
exclude capital gains?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The income inequality measure that I referred to is not one
measure, actually, it is a number of them. They are all set out in the document originally
commissioned by the previous Labour Government, which thought it was going to use it
as a political tool in Opposition to demonstrate that inequality was getting worse. But,
actually, it does not demonstrate that. Any measure of income inequality shows that it is
flat and vaguely falling. In respect of capital gains—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It was a very simple
question. It has already—
19 Jun 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 18719

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I agree with that, but the member rose to his feet just as the
Minister was about to address the portion about capital gains, and I would like to hear
that answer.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I understand that measure is aimed at income measures not
capital measures, and I cannot actually tell him whether it excludes capital gains, but it
probably does.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: Does he agree with Professor Jonathan Boston, co -author of
Child Poverty in New Zealand , who suggested that the poorest Kiwi children are now
no better off than some ch ildren in the slums of India, and what steps can be taken
towards introducing a living wage to address the immediate impacts of income
deprivation in too many New Zealand families?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, I certainly disagree with Dr Jona than Boston’s
comments and I think it discredits the campaign that he has been part of. If his advice to
New Zealand politicians is to copy conditions in Indian slums because children are
better off, then we certainly feel free to reject that advice. Secon dly, can I acknowledge
the Māori Party’s efforts over recent years. It has lobbied hard to increase the minimum
wage to the kinds of levels that the living wage has been set at. We just do not agree
with it going that high; we think it would destroy too ma ny jobs. But we do
acknowledge the intent of the Māori Party to help those who are on the lowest incomes.
Child Poverty—Government Initiatives to Address and Impact on Child Health
6. KEVIN HAGUE (Green)  to the Minister for Social Development : Does she
agree with Professor Jonathan Boston that there are New Zealand children living in
“houses that don’t have heating, in caravans that don’t have running water, and in
families that simply don’t have enough  food of the right kind every day”; if so, will she
guarantee these children have immediate access to the State support they need?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I agree that some
children in New Zealand are living in conditions that are unacceptable, but I do not
agree with Professor Jonathan Boston when he likens the living standards of our
children to the slums of India. If he thinks that this G overnment is going to follow the
policies of India and think that that is in any way acceptable, then I would completely
disagree, particularly when one looks at the mortality rates. The mortality rates for
under-fives in India is 56:1000, and in New Zealand—

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This is a question on notice, and
the Minister is speaking about Professor Boston’s comments about India, which was not
the topic of the primary question at all. I have asked the Minister  to address specifically
some specific comments of Jonathan Boston, which she has not done.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Minister has certainly specifically addressed the first part of the
question. There is a second part to the question that I am still wai ting for the Minister to
address, but it is unhelpful, when members are not getting an answer they like, to then
interject on the Minister before the Minister completes the answer. If the Minister then
completes the answer and it requires further addressin g, by all means raise the question.
I call on the Hon Paula Bennett to complete the answer.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: These children do get access to State support. There is
access through a very generous benefit and welfare system. There is a ccess to hardship
grants, on which we spend over $260 million a year. There is access to Warm Up New

items.speaker: Zealand
items.text: Healthy Homes. There is access to numerous types of support for these
children, including breakfast in schools.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Given t hat the Minister does not appear to agree with Professor
Boston, does she now agree with Otago University experts Dr Jean Simpson and Dr Liz
18720 Questions for Oral Answer 19 Jun 2014
Craig, whose research shows that one New Zealand baby dies each week from
conditions associated with low income?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I agree that there are some children in New Zealand who
are not living in the types of conditions that we would want them to. That is why in this
Budget, when we first had money available to be giving out, we gave it to families. That
is why we have prioritised those children. That is why we see a commitment to those
children through the Children’s Action Plan, through breakfast in schools, and through
more money for rheumatic fever, for warming up homes, for the many, many—

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am reluctant to do this, but once
again the Minister is not responding to the question at all, which—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Then I will help the member. If the member simply asks the
question, rather than the original paraphrase about whether the Minister does not appear
to agree with something, and simply asks the question whether the Minister agrees with
two Otago University experts about the death rate of young babies in New Zealand —if
the member blatantly asks that question without any peripheral information, then I can
perhaps try to assist the member to get an answer to his question. I will invite the
member to ask his question again.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Thank you. Does she now agree with Otago University experts Dr
Jean Simpson and Dr Liz Craig, whose research shows that one New Zealand baby each
week dies from conditions associated with low income?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: What I do agree with is that there are children living in
this country who are not living at the sorts of standards we think they should be.
However, we have one of the most generous welfare systems in the world. We have
availability of State housing. We are warming up those houses. We have breakfast in
schools for all schools that want that, and that is new under this Government in
partnership with those outside. We also have help for rheumatic fever. We have more
assistance for free doctors visits than ever before, and that is why in this Budget we
were able to give more than $500 million for further access for families and children.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My colleague Mr Hague
took your advice and rephrased the question in the manner in which you agreed—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And I invite Mr Hague to ask the question again.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: That’s pathetic.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That sort of comment from th e Government benches will
result in somebody leaving the Chamber.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Does she now agree with Otago University experts Dr Jean Simpson
and Dr Liz Craig, whose research shows one New Zealand baby each week dies from
conditions associated with low income?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: For me to make a judgment call on that, I would have to
look at the evidence behind the research. What I do agree with is that there are children
in New Zealand who are living in conditions that w e do not think are acceptable.
However, we have one of the most generous welfare systems in the world. They have
access to more health facilities for children under 13 now than ever before, and our
investment is very much on those children, but we cannot m ake judgments on
everyone’s choices all of the time either.

items.text: Does the Minister believe the experts when they tell us that poverty is

Biosecurity Management—Wallaceville Biocontainment Laboratory
8. IAN McKELVIE (National —Rangitīkei) to the Minister for Primary

items.speaker: Industries
items.text: What recent announcement has he made regarding the biocontainment
facility at Wallaceville?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: On Monday I announced
a $65 million high -security, biocontainment facility will be built in Wallaceville in
Upper Hutt. This is another demonstration of the Government’s commitment to
biosecurity. This new fit -for-purpose laboratory fac ility will be equipped to current
international standards and have better capacity to deal with large -scale emergency
situations in the unlikely event that one should occur. It will replace the existing high -
security laboratory at the site and continue mor e than 100 years of animal disease
diagnostics at this site. Work is expected to begin on the site next month, with
construction planned to begin early next year.

items.speaker: Ian McKelvie
items.text: Why is this announcement important for New Zealand’s primary
industry exports?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: Primary industries are the backbone of the New Zealand
economy, with over $20 billion worth of exports coming from animals and animal
products. A major disease outbreak could halt trade, which could be resum ed only
through extensive laboratory testing. The laboratories and skilled personnel at
Wallaceville have an essential role in responding to disease outbreaks, protecting public
health, and providing international trade assurances about New Zealand’s anima l
disease status. I have made biosecurity my No. 1 priority. A world -standard diagnostic
laboratory is not a luxury; indeed, it is a necessity.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Despite the commitment of the Labo ur Party to introduce a
broad-ranging sugar tax, made at a meeting at lunchtime today—

Transport Funding, Auckland—City Rail Link and Government Policy Statement
10. JULIE ANNE GENTER (Green) to the Minister of Transport: Does the draft
Government Policy Statement on transport funding identify any funding for the
Auckland City Rail Link in the transport budget over the next decade?

items.text: The Government Policy

Management Act 2003. It covers a period of 10 years, is released eve ry 3 years, and is

Statement on Land Transport  has never mentioned funding for the Auckland
electrification, the Wellington electrification extension, or the new electric trains for

Schools, Attendance Costs—Donations
11. CHRIS HIPKINS (Labour —Rimutaka) to the Minister of Education : Is she
satisfied that schools receive sufficient funding to deliver the New Zealand Curriculum;
if so, why?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Yes; because the Government is
investing more than $5 billion to support curriculum deliv ery in primary and secondary
education. Despite tight fiscal constraints, this Government has made year -on-year
increases through the last six Budgets and is now investing $10.1 billion in Vote
Education—the highest ever.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Why is she satisfied that school funding is sufficient to deliver the
curriculum, when parental donations to schools have increased by over 30 percent
during National’s watch, meaning parents are now forking out almost $100 million a
year in supposed donations to pay for their kids’ education?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I am satisfied, because we are investing just over $5
billion. What we do know, though, is that there has to be better discussions between
boards and their parent communities about wh at they expect over and above the
delivery of the curriculum. I do not have the specific figure to hand that indicates what

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Why does she believe that sc hools are sufficiently funded, given the
latest New Zealand Council for Educational Research national survey revealed that

items.text: I can but repeat my answer: it is because we are investing

are getting the achievement lifts across the system, and because we are investing in the
quality of teaching and learning, including  the initiative the Prime Minister announced
in January of an additional net new $359 million into the profession, whose members
are the key contributors to raising achievement.

funding the delivery of the school curriculum. We are seeing more achievement, and we

Powers of Attorney, Enduring—Report
12. ALFRED NGARO (National)on behalf of Hon PHIL HEATLEY (National—
Whangarei) to the Minister for Senior Citizens : What recent reports has she released
relating to enduring powers of attorney?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: I have recently released a
comprehensive review of the 2007 amendments to the enduring power of attorney
provisions in the Protection of  Personal and Property Rights Act 1998. The review
found that the 2007 amendments have for the most part been effective in providing
better protection for people setting up enduring powers of attorney, but it also identified
areas that need improving.
18728 Questions for Oral Answer 19 Jun 2014

items.speaker: Alfred Ngaro
items.text: What is she doing to address the recommendations in the report?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: After finding that there was generally low understanding as
to what an enduring power of attorney is, an information campaign will co mmence in
the coming weeks. This targets those appointing attorneys, people taking on the role of
enduring power of attorney, health practitioners, and legal professionals to understand
what is required of them. Work has already begun on simplifying the fo rms and
processes for applying for an enduring power of attorney, and I am also looking at
